title: Realizing That You Have Been Taken Advantage Of
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article walks through the discomfort of recognizing you've been taken advantage of in a relationship, listing telltale signs from unreciprocated help to stolen credit for ideas, and lays out the choices available once that recognition sets in. It emphasizes knowing your own non-negotiable boundaries first, then communicating them clearly, rather than simply absorbing the pattern or exiting quietly. For confrontation specifically, it recommends framing the conversation around the relationship you want rather than a list of past grievances, turning it into a collaborative discussion instead of a reproach. For the specific case of stolen credit, it offers a concrete documentation tactic — putting accomplishments in writing and sharing them broadly, including with the offending party — as a preventive measure.
points: Confronting an imbalanced relationship works best when framed around the relationship you want going forward, not a list of past grievances.
For stolen credit specifically, documenting accomplishments in writing and sharing them broadly (including with the offender) is offered as a concrete preventive tactic.
The piece argues that letting others know your boundaries is essential — silence tends to let the imbalanced pattern continue and eventually produce an emotional flare-up.
The closing distinction is pointed: being kind doesn't require being a doormat, and setting limits is framed as central to personal well-being.
quotes: A colleague or friend who never reciprocates. Scant communication or follow-up after you’ve helped someone out.
Once you realize you have been taken advantage of, the imperative question is what to do about it.
Describe the relationship you want to have as opposed to complaining about what has already transpired. Ask them to think along with you about ways to address the disparity you are feeling.
In the instance of someone taking credit for your ideas or results, document your accomplishments and proposals in emails and share them widely, including with the guilty party.
Good people take advantage of opportunities, not other people. That’s how you know they’re good people.
